Yeah, I'll be presenting today. Janann. Thank you, Janann. Okay, great. Good morning. My name is Janann Cato with the Zoning Administration Division. I'm joined by Leslie Johnson, Bill Mayland, and Tracy Strunk. We'll be presenting on the proposed zoning ordinance amendment for congregate living facilities. We also have a staff summary document with additional details and the

draft text we're proposing. Our hope today is to gather more input and feedback as we move forward with the amendment. For background, this amendment originates from the 2025 Zoning Ordinance Work Program, which the board endorsed in June. Congregate living facilities were identified as a priority one item directing staff to review zoning provisions for congregate living facilities to potentially expand the districts where they're allowed and revise the definition and standards to include uses like homeless shelters and supportive housing. And this direction builds on past

discussions. So the Housing Committee in November 2022 directed staff to look at zoning barriers for facilities serving people experiencing homelessness. The 2025 work program item was carried forward from an earlier work program topic in 2023-2024 and a December 2022 board matter that flagged this need. So this amendment is intended to revise the definition of congregate living facilities and provide more flexibility in where they can be located.

Under today's ordinance, a congregate living facility is defined as housing in a supervised setting with on-site counselors or staff. They may include inpatient alcohol and addiction treatment and services for more than eight persons with disabilities.

A certified recovery residence with over eight residents might also fall under this definition. And the definition clarifies that congregate living facilities are distinct from group households, assisted living facilities, and group residential facilities.

Those are different uses that are limited by age, disability, or resident count. By contrast, congregate living facilities can serve more diverse populations with broader supportive needs and don't have a maximum resident count under the zoning ordinance.

And that distinction means that congregate living facilities serve populations that don't fit neatly into other categories. Currently, congregate living facilities are permitted with special exception approval in all conventional residential districts except for rural agricultural as well as in commercial districts C1 through C4. In plan districts, they must either be shown on the development plan or approved by special exception. There's also a location standard which stipulates that if the facility looks like a single-family detached house, it follows that

district standards. Otherwise, it must be located at least 100 feet from all lot lines that abut the R1 through R4 residential districts and 45 feet from all other lot lines or as determined by the board. The congregate living facility used was first added to the zoning ordinance in 2003 through an amendment. The amendment replaced the older use, which was called institutions providing housing and general care to the indigent orphans and the like. The term was updated to remove

outdated terms and to reflect the broad range of support services that could be provided in a congregate living environment. Since that time, in 2003, there have been six special exceptions approved. Each one has been in a residential district. The facilities serve a range of populations, including survivors of human trafficking, women escaping domestic violence, adolescents with eating disorders, and one facility for retired and current priests.

The draft text for the proposed amendment revises and clarifies the definition. The new language identifies the range of populations served, including persons experiencing homelessness, survivors of violence or abuse, youth in crisis, families in medical crises, facilities that don't meet the state code requirements for a group residential facility due to the services provided or the number of residents.

Also, certified recovery residences with more than eight residents. The current definition only specifies alcohol and addiction treatment and treatment for more than eight persons with disabilities. By identifying these populations, the ordinance will better reflect the facilities already operating, and it also ensures clarity for applicants and for staff and distinguishes this use from others like assisted living facilities or group residential facilities.

The draft text expands permissions into additional districts, still by special exception. Specifically, congregate living facilities could be considered in commercial districts C5 through C8 and industrial districts I2 through I4.

And the intent here is flexibility. These districts may offer additional and possibly larger sites, more affordable land, or opportunities for adaptive reuse of vacant buildings. and many are located near transit and community services, which would help residents connect with resources. We're not proposing to extend permissions into the heavier I-5 and I-6 industrial districts because those areas are less compatible with residential uses.

With expanding the permissions, we also want to maintain compatibility with surrounding land uses, so we're proposing additional development standards. The intent with the development standards is to strike a balance of flexibility and compatibility with residential. They aren't intended to impose new requirements, but rather to codify current approaches. So first, we're proposing that facilities in commercial and industrial districts must be located near public transit, community services, and employment areas so that residents can reasonably access

opportunities and support. Second, we're also proposing that congregate living facilities may not be located in the three areas designated as industrial on the comprehensive plan concept for future development map in the comprehensive plan. And this preserves industrial land while still allowing congregate living facilities in I-district locations that are planned for mixed-use centers. Third, we're proposing a development standard that requires on-site staff and supportive services, except with a recovery residence. And these services,

such as case management, transportation assistance, or health care support, ensures that residents are receiving the needed services and assistance to improve outcomes. Finally, a new submission requirement would require applicants to describe the population served, the number of residents and staff, the services offered, the length of stay, licensing, and intake criteria. This would provide a clear picture when reviewing applications and ensure transparency about the

facility's purpose.
